The split calculation gives a precise information requirement. One exterior-field value at each distinct enclosed zero determines the block polynomial’s instantaneous velocity, even at repeated zeros. Evolving those values requires more exterior information. I’m now checking how that distinction affects the gap and its forcing.

The local equations passed a separate internal review. Pairing one exterior zero on each side of the gap also exposes a cancellation that separate distance bounds lose. I’m testing what survives when all omitted zeros are included, particularly nonreal zeros whose contributions can have either sign.

The spatial estimate now accounts for the full exterior. It identifies a region where even a nonreal zero contributes favorably, so only a bounded neighborhood can lower the forcing on a fixed-width strip. That gives a finite test on a previously counted pair near heights 28 and 42: whether one neighboring zero can establish the sign of the gap’s acceleration.

The high-height result passed internal review. On any fixed slab bounded away from time zero, the complete forcing approaches its equally spaced value uniformly, even if some low zeros are nonreal. I’m now running the separate finite test near heights 28 and 42, with a direct derivative calculation for comparison.

The branch now has a separate plan for predicting individual zero positions. I’ll make that the primary continuation in the handoff. The adjacent-gap curvature test will remain available as a narrower follow-up to this session’s spacing result.

Direct evaluation on the same interval gives the tighter enclosure \(0.01051532122<g''(t)<0.01090242033\). A separate internal replay reproduced every numerical result.
